The request

Subject: Weekend staffing: a checked KPI before the next scheduling cycle
RO
Regional Operations Director
To: Regional Operations Analyst (you)
Cc: the scheduling team

Hi Operations Analytics team,

Before I set the next staffing cycle, I need a checked view of our recent delivery performance. The latest dashboard looks below target, and weekend staffing has already been suggested as the reason. Warm up on five short practice cases (other organizations, made-up numbers), each followed by the same check on our MetroMeal figures. Then build the real KPI from our delivery file.

Specifically, I need answers to 14 questions:

  1. 1. Practice: what decision can HarborCare's KPI inform?
    Frame the clinic manager's decision and check the no-show rate against its target and guardrail.
    Part A
  2. 2. Is our latest week below target?
    Use the slide numbers for the latest week. Tell me the on-time rate, the gap in percentage points, and the complaint rate.
    Part B
  3. 3. Practice: is NorthLine's KPI reproducible?
    Could another analyst get the same number from your definition alone?
    Part C
  4. 4. What is our four-week rate?
    Build it from counts, not from an average of weekly percentages.
    Part D
  5. 5. Practice: what does one BrightCart row represent?
    Classify the fields and warn me about the order-to-item join.
    Part E
  6. 6. How many orders hide in our joined rows?
    Show me the difference between joined rows and distinct orders.
    Part F
  7. 7. Practice: is RiverTown's chart honest?
    Name what is misleading and how you would fix it.
    Part G
  8. 8. What is wrong with our dashboard chart?
    It says performance collapses. Check the scale, the colors and the title.
    Part H
  9. 9. Practice: is GreenBlock's story bounded?
    Separate what the records show from what the draft claims.
    Part I
  10. 10. Can every number in our story be traced?
    Verify at least one number a second way before it goes in the story.
    Part J
  11. 11. What does one row of our delivery file represent?
    Confirm the key, the grain and which deliveries are eligible.
    Part K
  12. 12. How did each week compare with the target and the complaint guardrail?
    Build the weekly table from the raw rows and check the late deliveries in the latest week.
    Part L
  13. 13. Can you give me one honest chart?
    Linked to your checked numbers, with a zero baseline, labels, denominators and the target line.
    Part M
  14. 14. Does the evidence support investigating weekend staffing?
    Three sentences: what it shows, what it does not show, and what I should do next. Do not claim a cause the records cannot show.
    Part N

Please send me:

  • your saved practice workbook (nothing to upload; this is ungraded practice), and
  • three bounded sentences in Response!B7 that the instructor may read aloud for feedback.

Our delivery file and the practice workbook are attached. Thanks. I want an answer I can defend, not a guess.

Best,
Regional Operations Director
MetroMeal Delivery

Before class: get ready (untimed)

  1. Unzip S02P_Student_Package.zip into one folder.
    Keep every file together. SPSS looks for orders_story.csv next to the syntax.
  2. Open S02P_Learning_Workbook.xlsx, read Start_Here, then save a copy with your own name.
    Pattern: S02P_FirstName_LastName_NetID.xlsx (NetID is the part before @nyu.edu).
  3. Open S02P_SPSS.sps in SPSS and fix line 7.
    Replace CHANGE_TO_YOUR_EXTRACTED_LAB_FOLDER with your folder's path.
  4. Select the first block (Import orders_story.csv) and choose Run › Selection.
✅ Ready when: SPSS reports 2,000 eligible completed deliveries and your workbook is saved under your own name.
⚠️ Stuck? Ask for help before the first practice. This session is ungraded practice.

Find your folder path (for the CD line)

SPSS needs the path of the folder you unzipped, the one that holds S02P_SPSS.sps and the CSV files. It is not the path to the .sps file. If you open the folder and see the .sps file and the CSV files inside, that is the right folder.

Windows
  1. Unzip first: right-click S02P_Student_Package.zip › Extract All › Extract. Do not work inside the zip.
  2. Open the extracted S02P_Student_Package folder, then the Student folder inside it. You should now see S02P_SPSS.sps and the CSV files. This is your lab folder.
  3. Click once in the address bar at the top of File Explorer: it turns into the path. Press Ctrl+C.
  4. Or: go up one level, hold Shift, right-click that folder › Copy as path, then delete the double quotes it adds.

Looks like C:\Users\you\Downloads\S02P_Student_Package\Student

Mac
  1. Unzip first: double-click S02P_Student_Package.zip in Finder.
  2. Open the extracted S02P_Student_Package folder, then the Student folder inside it. You should now see S02P_SPSS.sps and the CSV files. This is your lab folder.
  3. Go up one level and click that folder once to select it (the folder, not a file inside it). Press Option+Command+C (Copy as Pathname), or right-click it, hold Option and choose Copy … as Pathname.

Looks like /Users/you/Downloads/S02P_Student_Package/Student

Paste it between the single quotes on the CD line:

CD 'C:\Users\you\Downloads\S02P_Student_Package\Student'.      * Windows
CD '/Users/you/Downloads/S02P_Student_Package/Student'.          * Mac
⚠️ Common mistakes: the path ends in /S02P_SPSS.sps (remove the file name); the quotes or the final period are missing; the files are still inside the zip; OneDrive or iCloud has not finished downloading the folder. If H0 says a file cannot be found, check the path first. If the path itself contains an apostrophe ('), put the path in double quotes instead, for example CD "/Users/you/Kim's files/S02P_Student_Package/Student".

Part A · What decision can the KPI inform?

⏱ 3 min
From slide 19 → work this card → Back to slide 20 · bring: One bounded decision question, one supported descriptive claim, and one causal claim to remove.

What the session covered · Section 1 Decision Frame and Running-Case Brief

Start with the decision, not the chart. Name who acts, what they might do, and by when. Then name the measures:

  • KPI: the measure you monitor. Here: the monthly no-show rate. rate=qualifying counteligible count \text{rate} = \dfrac{\text{qualifying count}}{\text{eligible count}}
  • Target: the benchmark for the KPI. HarborCare wants no more than 10.0% no-shows.
  • Guardrail: a limit that protects a different outcome. Complaints must stay at or below 4.0%.
  • Evidence boundary: one month of counts can show a level. It cannot show a trend or a cause.

HarborCare is a made-up clinic. Its numbers are not part of the MetroMeal data.

Stuck? Three quick fixes
  • B16 does not show 3.0%. Divide complaints by eligible appointments: =B14/B13, not by no-shows.
  • B15 shows #DIV/0!. B13 is still empty. Type 400 in B13.
  • B15 shows 0.115. Choose Home › Percent Style, then set one decimal place.
Why can't one month show that performance is worsening?

"Worsening" compares two periods. You have only one month, so there is nothing to compare against. Ask for an earlier month with the same KPI definition. Even then, a change over time does not show why it changed.

Part B · Is MetroMeal's latest week below target?

⏱ 3 min
From slide 19 → work this card → Back to slide 20 · bring: One bounded decision question, one supported descriptive claim, and one causal claim to remove.

What the session covered · Section 1 Decision Frame and Running-Case Brief

Same frame, now with the MetroMeal numbers from the slides. The director may investigate weekend staffing before the next scheduling cycle.

  • On-time rate: the KPI. 392 392 on time out of 500 500 eligible deliveries.
  • Target gap: the direct difference from the 85.0% target, in percentage points. (rate−T)×100 (\text{rate} - T) \times 100
  • Complaint guardrail: complaints among the same 500 deliveries must stay at or below 3.0%.

sheet Class_Practice · answers email question 3

Part C · Is the KPI calculation reproducible?

⏱ 3 min
From slide 38 → work this card → Back to slide 39 · bring: A checked KPI formula with units, visible numerator and denominator, target gap, and one limitation.

What the session covered · Section 2 Operational KPI Definitions and Statistical Meaning

A KPI is reproducible when another analyst could compute the same number from your definition alone. Write down:

  • Population and window: which records count, and when. Here: eligible NorthLine support calls in September 2026.
  • Numerator and denominator: calls resolved within 5 minutes, over all eligible calls. rate=684760 \text{rate} = \dfrac{684}{760}
  • Direction and target: higher is better; the target is at least 92.0%.
  • Count or proportion: a count shows workload; a proportion compares performance across eligible opportunities.

Stuck? Three quick fixes
  • B24 shows a number like 46266. Format B24:B25 as dates: Home › Number › Short Date.
  • B31 shows -0.02. Multiply the difference by 100: =(B30-B23)*100.
  • B30 shows 111.1%. The division is upside down. Use =B21/B22, qualifying over eligible.
Why write a full KPI specification? (optional)

The same words, "resolution rate", can hide different populations, windows and rules. The specification in B34 pins them down: purpose, unit, population, September window, one call per row, eligibility, calculation, higher-is-better, the 92.0% target and a refresh schedule.

sheet Slide_Practice · answers email question 4

Part D · What is the four-week on-time rate, built from counts?

⏱ 3 min
From slide 38 → work this card → Back to slide 39 · bring: A checked KPI formula with units, visible numerator and denominator, target gap, and one limitation.

What the session covered · Section 2 Operational KPI Definitions and Statistical Meaning

To combine weeks, add the counts first, then divide. This is count-first aggregation.

  • Weekly rate: ratew=Ow/Ew \text{rate}_w = O_w / E_w for each week w w .
  • Overall rate: ∑Ow/∑Ew \sum O_w \big/ \sum E_w . Each delivery counts once.
  • Why not average the rates?: an average of rates gives every week equal weight, even when one week has many more deliveries.

Slides 20–37
Reproducible KPI Specification 21–22 · Count, Proportion, and Target Gap 23–25 · Percentage Points vs Percent Change 26–27 · Reproduce the KPI in Excel 365 28 · Aggregation from Counts 32–34

pp. 8–12
Reproducible KPI specification p. 8
Full Toolkit
pp. 18–31
Reproducible KPI specification p. 31

The equations you are building

Ow O_w = on-time deliveries in week w w · Ew E_w = eligible deliveries in week w w
Four-week rate=∑w=14Ow∑w=14Ew=SUM(B21:B24)SUM(B25:B28) \text{Four-week rate} = \frac{\sum_{w=1}^{4} O_w}{\sum_{w=1}^{4} E_w} = \frac{\text{SUM(B21:B24)}}{\text{SUM(B25:B28)}}

Stuck? Three quick fixes

Why does count-first matter when weeks differ? (optional)90%+75%2=82.5%≠90+300100+400=390500=78.0% \frac{90\% + 75\%}{2} = 82.5\% \quad\neq\quad \frac{90 + 300}{100 + 400} = \frac{390}{500} = 78.0\%

Suppose week 1 has 90 of 100 on time (90.0%) and week 2 has 300 of 400 (75.0%). The average of the two rates is 82.5%. But only 390 of 500 deliveries were on time, which is 78.0%. The bigger week should carry more weight, and summing counts does that automatically.

Part E · What does one row represent?

⏱ 3 min
From slide 54 → work this card → Back to slide 55 · bring: A completed type-and-scale classification, two grain statements, and one mixed-grain warning.

What the session covered · Section 3 Variables, Measurement Scales, Observations, and Grain

Before you count anything, finish the sentence "Each row represents one ...". That is the table's grain.

  • Data type: categorical (labels, codes, flags) or numerical (discrete counts, continuous measures).
  • Measurement scale: nominal (names only), ordinal (ordered), interval, or ratio (true zero, ratios make sense).
  • Analytical role: identifier, measure, category, ordered category or flag.
  • Join risk: joining orders (one row per order) to items (one row per item) gives one row per item. Orders with many items repeat.

Whose experience gets extra weight after the join? (optional)

An order with three items appears three times, so its outcome counts three times in an order-level rate. Customers who buy more items quietly get more say. Restoring one row per order gives every order one vote again.

Part F · How many orders hide in four joined rows?

⏱ 3 min
From slide 54 → work this card → Back to slide 55 · bring: A completed type-and-scale classification, two grain statements, and one mixed-grain warning.

What the session covered · Section 3 Variables, Measurement Scales, Observations, and Grain

MetroMeal's source file has one row per eligible completed delivery. The weekly table has one row per week. Aggregating changes what a row can support.

  • Raw grain: 2,000 rows, one per eligible completed delivery.
  • Summary grain: 4 rows, one per week.
  • Key test: if the number of rows equals the number of distinct keys, the key is unique at that grain.

Part G · Does the chart communicate honestly?

⏱ 3 min
From slide 70 → work this card → Back to slide 71 · bring: One statistical defect, one accessibility defect, one repair, and a revised bounded title.

What the session covered · Section 4 Chart Selection and Honest Statistical Critique

Check the numbers first, then the picture. An honest chart shows the checked values without exaggeration.

  • Baseline: bars are read by length, so the bar axis starts at 0%.
  • Denominators: show n n next to each rate. The same rate can rest on very different amounts of evidence.
  • Accessibility: never rely on red and green alone. Add a label, pattern or outline.
  • Title: state what was observed. "Demand will continue falling" is a forecast three months cannot support.

Part H · What makes the MetroMeal dashboard chart misleading?

⏱ 3 min
From slide 70 → work this card → Back to slide 71 · bring: One statistical defect, one accessibility defect, one repair, and a revised bounded title.

What the session covered · Section 4 Chart Selection and Honest Statistical Critique

The dashboard chart starts its bars at 75.0%, drops the denominators, uses red and green alone, and says performance collapses.

  • Truncated axis: on a 75% to 90% axis, the 78.4% bar looks tiny next to 87.6%. On a 0% to 100% axis the difference is honest.
  • Every phrase from a checked cell: the repaired title quotes the rate and gap you verify in B68 and B69.
  • Four points: show an observed sequence. They do not show a stable trend or a forecast.

Part I · Is the data story traceable and bounded?

⏱ 3 min
From slide 78 → work this card → Back to slide 79 · bring: One explanatory title, a three-sentence bounded story, one action, one limitation, and one next validation check.

What the session covered · Section 5 Bounded Story, Validation, and Bridge to Descriptive Evidence

A bounded story says only what the records can support. It links the audience, the checked result, the comparison, an action, a limitation and a next check.

  • Supported: the observed rate and its gap to target, for the stated period.
  • Not supported: "the new policy caused the miss". Three descriptive months cannot isolate a cause.
  • Bounded action: investigate before revising.

Part J · Can every number in the MetroMeal story be traced?

From slide 78 → work this card → Back to slide 79 · bring: One explanatory title, a three-sentence bounded story, one action, one limitation, and one next validation check.

What the session covered · Section 5 Bounded Story, Validation, and Bridge to Descriptive Evidence

Before a number goes into the story, check it a second way. Validation follows the chain from counts to rate, gap and guardrail.

  • Reconcile: on-time plus late must equal eligible: 392+108−500=0 392 + 108 - 500 = 0 .
  • Recompute: divide 14/500 14 / 500 yourself instead of copying 2.8% from a dashboard.
  • Keep it bounded: four descriptive weeks can justify investigating staffing, not changing it.

Part K · What does one row of the MetroMeal file represent?

⏱ 4 min
Guided build · starts at slide 80, back to slide 82

What the session covered · Section 3 Variables, Measurement Scales, Observations, and Grain

The guided build starts at slide 80. The instructor models this step. Look at Orders_Story first: the data sit in an Excel table named Orders.

  • Grain: each row is one eligible completed delivery, August 3 to August 30, 2026.
  • Candidate key: order_id is a key if rows and distinct IDs are equal: Nrows=Ndistinct N_{\text{rows}} = N_{\text{distinct}} .
  • Eligibility: eligible_kpi_flag is 1 when a delivery belongs in the denominator. Summing a 0/1 flag counts the 1s.
  • Decision frame: write it in Guided_Practice!B5 before you calculate anything.

Part L · How did each week compare with the target and the guardrail?

⏱ 4 min
Guided build · starts at slide 80, back to slide 82

What the session covered · Section 2 Operational KPI Definitions and Statistical Meaning

Build one row per week (rows 7 to 10), a count-first total (row 11) and late-delivery checks for the latest week (row 18).

  • Weekly rate: ratew=Ow/Ew \text{rate}_w = O_w / E_w , with the eligible count in column C and the on-time count in column D.
  • Target gap: (ratew−T)×100 (\text{rate}_w - T) \times 100 in percentage points. $B$14 stays fixed when you fill down.
  • Guardrail: Cw/Ew C_w / E_w , complaints over the same eligible deliveries.
  • Late minutes: the mean uses every delay; the median is the middle; the 90th percentile shows the long tail.

A mean above the median is a reason to look at the distribution. It is not proof of a cause.

F11 pools all four weeks: 1,675 of 2,000 deliveries were on time, 83.75%. Three strong weeks hide the weak latest week. That is why the director needs the weekly rows, not only the total.

What the session covered · Section 4 Chart Selection and Honest Statistical Critique

Link the chart table to KPI_Build so the chart updates when a number is fixed. Then build a column-and-line combo chart.

  • Linked, not typed: every source cell starts with =KPI_Build!.
  • Zero baseline: set the vertical axis to Minimum 0 and Maximum 1 (0% to 100%).
  • Direct labels: label each bar with its rate and n n , using the text built in E5:E8.
  • Non-color cue: give the latest bar a pattern fill or a thick outline, so it shows in grayscale.

To build the chart: select A4:C8, choose Insert › Combo Chart › Clustered Column: Line. Make On-time rate the columns and Target the line, both on the primary axis. For labels, choose Format Data Labels › Value From Cells, select E5:E8, and clear the plain Value box.

Topic 1 · Reproduce the practice Reproduce

Same question in Excel → SPSS → Python → R.

Excel Parts A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J, K, L, M, N

No code needed: your workbook is the Excel version. Open Self_Check. Every row should show a tick. Then check these numbers in KPI_Build: 2,000 rows, latest on-time rate 78.4%, gap -6.6 points, complaint rate 2.8%, four-week rate 83.75%, and in row 18: 108 late deliveries with mean 12.4, median 7 and 90th percentile 31 minutes. Type your Excel values into column C of Compare_Tools, rows 7 to 13.

SPSS Parts A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J, K, L, M, N

No new code. Run S02P_SPSS.sps one block at a time. Guided Step 1 should show 2,000 eligible rows. Guided Step 2 lists the weekly table (latest 78.4%, gap -6.6) and the four-week aggregate (83.75%), then describes the 108 late deliveries. Hand-off Blocks H1 to H5 redo the typed practice cases. Type the SPSS values into column D of Compare_Tools. SPSS uses a different percentile rule from PERCENTILE.INC, so its 90th percentile can differ a little from 31.

Python Parts A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J, K, L, M, N

Recomputes every practice rate, the weekly KPI table, the count-first aggregate, the late-delivery checks and the chart labels. It also saves the repaired Part M chart as S02P_repaired_chart.png: zero baseline, labels with n, a dashed target line and a hatch pattern on the latest bar. Your printed numbers should match the workbook: 78.4%, -6.6, 2.8%, 83.75%, 108 late, 12.4 / 7.0 / 31.0 minutes. Runs in Colab or any Python with pandas and matplotlib.

# S02P Parts A-N in Python (optional, not graded).
# Put this file next to orders_story.csv.
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")                     # save the chart to a file; no window needed
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.ticker import PercentFormatter
import pandas as pd

def pct(x, d=1):
    return f"{x:.{d}%}"

def gap(rate, target):                    # percentage points, not percent change
    return (rate - target) * 100

# ---- Parts A-J: the five practice cases (typed numbers) ----
print("A HarborCare  no-show rate  =", pct(46 / 400), "| complaint rate =", pct(12 / 400))
print("B MetroMeal   on-time rate  =", pct(392 / 500),
      "| gap =", f"{gap(392 / 500, 0.85):.1f}", "pp | complaint rate =", pct(14 / 500))
print("C NorthLine   resolution    =", pct(684 / 760),
      "| gap =", f"{gap(684 / 760, 0.92):.1f}", "pp")
weeks_on_time, weeks_eligible = [420, 438, 425, 392], [500, 500, 500, 500]
print("D MetroMeal   four-week rate =", pct(sum(weeks_on_time) / sum(weeks_eligible), 2),
      "(sum counts, then divide)")
print("E BrightCart  joined rows    =", 310, "item rows for", 120, "orders")
items = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": ["A", "A", "A", "B"],
                      "item_id": ["I1", "I2", "I3", "I4"]})
print("F Joined rows =", len(items), "| distinct orders =", items["order_id"].nunique())
cases = [(72, 80), (54, 60), (30, 50)]
print("G RiverTown   rates =", ", ".join(pct(a / e) for a, e in cases))
print("H MetroMeal   latest rate =", pct(0.784), "| gap =", f"{gap(0.784, 0.85):.1f}", "pp")
print("I GreenBlock  completion =", pct(273 / 300),
      "| gap =", f"{gap(273 / 300, 0.95):.1f}", "pp")
print("J MetroMeal   reconcile 392 + 108 - 500 =", 392 + 108 - 500)

# ---- Part K: source, key, grain and eligibility ----
df = pd.read_csv("orders_story.csv")
print("\nK Rows =", len(df), "| distinct order_id =", df["order_id"].nunique(),
      "| eligible =", int(df["eligible_kpi_flag"].sum()))
target, guardrail = df["target_rate"].max(), df["complaint_guardrail"].max()

# ---- Part L: weekly KPI table, count-first aggregate, latest late checks ----
elig = df[df["eligible_kpi_flag"] == 1]
weekly = elig.groupby("week_start").agg(eligible=("order_id", "size"),
                                        on_time=("on_time_kpi_flag", "sum"),
                                        complaints=("complaint_flag", "sum"))
weekly["rate"] = weekly["on_time"] / weekly["eligible"]
weekly["gap_pp"] = gap(weekly["rate"], target)
weekly["complaint_rate"] = weekly["complaints"] / weekly["eligible"]
print("\nL Weekly KPI table")
formats = {"rate": pct, "complaint_rate": pct, "gap_pp": "{:.1f}".format}
print(weekly.to_string(formatters=formats))
total = weekly[["eligible", "on_time", "complaints"]].sum()
overall = total["on_time"] / total["eligible"]
print("Four-week aggregate:", int(total["on_time"]), "/", int(total["eligible"]),
      "=", pct(overall, 2), "| gap =", f"{gap(overall, target):.2f}", "pp",
      "| complaints =", int(total["complaints"]),
      "=", pct(total["complaints"] / total["eligible"], 2))
latest = weekly.index.max()
is_late = (elig["week_start"] == latest) & (elig["late_minutes"] > 0)
late = elig.loc[is_late, "late_minutes"]
row = weekly.loc[latest]
print("Latest week", latest, ": late =", len(late), "| mean =", round(late.mean(), 1),
      "| median =", late.median(),
      "| 90th percentile =", late.quantile(0.9),        # same as PERCENTILE.INC
      "| reconcile =", int(row["eligible"] - row["on_time"] - len(late)))
ok = row["rate"] < target and row["complaint_rate"] <= guardrail
print("Decision check:", "Investigate, guardrail within limit" if ok
      else "Review KPI and guardrail")

# ---- Part M: direct labels for the chart ----
labels = [f"{pct(r)} (n = {n})" for r, n in zip(weekly["rate"], weekly["eligible"])]
print("\nM Labels:", ", ".join(labels))

# ---- Part M: the repaired chart, saved as a PNG ----
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
bars = ax.bar(weekly.index, weekly["rate"], color="#9aa9c9", edgecolor="black")
bars[-1].set_hatch("//")                  # non-color cue on the latest week
ax.axhline(target, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5,
           label=f"Target {target:.1%}")
for bar, r, label in zip(bars, weekly["rate"], labels):
    ax.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2, r + 0.02, label, ha="center", fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)                         # zero baseline for bars
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(1.0))
ax.set_ylabel("On-time rate")
ax.set_title("Latest observed weekly on-time rate was below the 85.0% target")
ax.legend(loc="lower left")
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("S02P_repaired_chart.png", dpi=150)
print("Saved S02P_repaired_chart.png")
R Parts A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J, K, L, M, N

The same checks in base R, plus the repaired chart saved as S02P_repaired_chart_r.png. quantile(type = 7) matches Excel's PERCENTILE.INC, so the 90th percentile should print 31.

# S02P Parts A-N in R (optional, not graded). Base R only.
# Put this file next to orders_story.csv.
pct <- function(x, d = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), 100 * x)
gap <- function(rate, target) (rate - target) * 100      # percentage points
g1 <- function(rate, target) sprintf("%.1f", gap(rate, target))

# ---- Parts A-J: the five practice cases (typed numbers) ----
cat("A HarborCare no-show rate =", pct(46 / 400), "| complaint rate =", pct(12 / 400), "\n")
cat("B MetroMeal on-time rate =", pct(392 / 500), "| gap =", g1(392 / 500, 0.85),
    "pp | complaint rate =", pct(14 / 500), "\n")
cat("C NorthLine resolution =", pct(684 / 760), "| gap =", g1(684 / 760, 0.92), "pp\n")
on_time_w <- c(420, 438, 425, 392); eligible_w <- rep(500, 4)
cat("D MetroMeal four-week rate =", pct(sum(on_time_w) / sum(eligible_w), 2), "\n")
cat("E BrightCart joined rows =", 310, "item rows for", 120, "orders\n")
items <- data.frame(order_id = c("A", "A", "A", "B"), item_id = c("I1", "I2", "I3", "I4"))
cat("F Joined rows =", nrow(items),
    "| distinct orders =", length(unique(items$order_id)), "\n")
cat("G RiverTown rates =", pct(c(72, 54, 30) / c(80, 60, 50)), "\n")
cat("H MetroMeal latest rate =", pct(0.784), "| gap =", g1(0.784, 0.85), "pp\n")
cat("I GreenBlock completion =", pct(273 / 300), "| gap =", g1(273 / 300, 0.95), "pp\n")
cat("J MetroMeal reconcile 392 + 108 - 500 =", 392 + 108 - 500, "\n")

# ---- Part K: source, key, grain and eligibility ----
df <- read.csv("orders_story.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cat("\nK Rows =", nrow(df), "| distinct order_id =", length(unique(df$order_id)),
    "| eligible =", sum(df$eligible_kpi_flag), "\n")
target <- max(df$target_rate); guardrail <- max(df$complaint_guardrail)

# ---- Part L: weekly KPI table, aggregate and latest late checks ----
elig <- df[df$eligible_kpi_flag == 1, ]
weekly <- aggregate(cbind(on_time = on_time_kpi_flag, complaints = complaint_flag,
                          eligible = eligible_kpi_flag) ~ week_start,
                    data = elig, FUN = sum)
weekly$rate <- weekly$on_time / weekly$eligible
weekly$gap_pp <- round(gap(weekly$rate, target), 1)
weekly$complaint_rate <- weekly$complaints / weekly$eligible
print(transform(weekly, rate = pct(rate), complaint_rate = pct(complaint_rate)))
overall <- sum(weekly$on_time) / sum(weekly$eligible)
cat("Four-week aggregate:", sum(weekly$on_time), "/", sum(weekly$eligible),
    "=", pct(overall, 2), "| gap =", sprintf("%.2f", gap(overall, target)), "pp",
    "| complaints =", sum(weekly$complaints),
    "=", pct(sum(weekly$complaints) / sum(weekly$eligible), 2), "\n")
latest <- max(weekly$week_start)                 # ISO dates sort correctly as text
late <- elig$late_minutes[elig$week_start == latest & elig$late_minutes > 0]
last <- weekly[weekly$week_start == latest, ]
p90 <- quantile(late, 0.9, type = 7, names = FALSE)   # type 7 = PERCENTILE.INC
cat("Latest week", latest, ": late =", length(late), "| mean =", round(mean(late), 1),
    "| median =", median(late), "| 90th percentile =", p90,
    "| reconcile =", last$eligible - last$on_time - length(late), "\n")
ok <- last$rate < target & last$complaint_rate <= guardrail
cat("Decision check:", ifelse(ok, "Investigate, guardrail within limit",
                              "Review KPI and guardrail"), "\n")

# ---- Part M: direct labels for the chart ----
labels <- paste0(pct(weekly$rate), " (n = ", weekly$eligible, ")")
cat("\nM Labels:", labels, sep = "\n  ")

# ---- Part M: the repaired chart, saved as a PNG ----
png("S02P_repaired_chart_r.png", width = 900, height = 520)
mids <- barplot(weekly$rate, names.arg = weekly$week_start,
                ylim = c(0, 1),                          # zero baseline
                col = "#9aa9c9", density = c(-1, -1, -1, 20),   # hatch the latest week
                ylab = "On-time rate",
                main = "Latest observed weekly on-time rate was below the 85.0% target")
abline(h = target, lty = 2, lwd = 2)
text(mids, weekly$rate + 0.04, labels)
legend("bottomleft", legend = paste("Target", pct(target)), lty = 2, lwd = 2, bg = "white")
dev.off()
cat("\nSaved S02P_repaired_chart_r.png\n")

Topic 2 · Weekday and weekend on-time rates, week by week Extend

Same question in Excel → SPSS → Python → R.

Excel Parts L

Click inside the Orders table and choose Insert › PivotTable › New Worksheet. Put week_start in Rows and weekend_flag in Columns. If Excel groups the dates into months, right-click a date and choose Ungroup. Put on_time_kpi_flag in Values three times: Sum (on-time count), Count (denominator) and Average (the average of a 0/1 flag is the on-time rate; format it as a percentage). The latest week should show 320 of 358 (89.4%) on weekdays and 72 of 142 (50.7%) on weekends. Write one bounded sentence about it.

SPSS Parts L

The crosstab shows on-time counts and row percentages for weekdays and weekends in each week. Compare the latest week with the earlier three.

New code: paste it at the end of S02P_SPSS.sps, make sure the setup has run this session, then select only the pasted lines and choose Run › Selection.

* Extension: on-time deliveries by weekend flag within each week.
* Run the import block first so OrdersStory is open.
DATASET ACTIVATE OrdersStory.
TEMPORARY.
SELECT IF (eligible_kpi_flag=1).
CROSSTABS
  /TABLES=weekend_flag BY on_time_kpi_flag BY week_start
  /CELLS=COUNT ROW.
Python Parts L

Split each week's on-time rate into weekday and weekend deliveries, with every denominator. Then ask: does a lower weekend rate show that staffing caused it? What else differs on weekends?

# Extension: is the latest dip concentrated on weekends? (descriptive only)
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("orders_story.csv")
elig = df[df["eligible_kpi_flag"] == 1]
table = elig.pivot_table(index="week_start", columns="weekend_flag",
                         values="on_time_kpi_flag", aggfunc=["sum", "count"])
for week in table.index:
    parts = []
    for flag, name in [(0, "weekday"), (1, "weekend")]:
        on_time, n = table.loc[week, ("sum", flag)], table.loc[week, ("count", flag)]
        parts.append(f"{name} {on_time}/{n} = {on_time / n:.1%}")
    print(week, " | ".join(parts))
print("Question: does this show that weekend staffing *caused* the dip?")
print("What else differs on weekends?")
R Parts L

The same split in base R with tapply(). The latest week should show weekday 320/358 = 89.4% and weekend 72/142 = 50.7%.

# Extension: is the latest dip concentrated on weekends? (descriptive only)
# Base R only.
df <- read.csv("orders_story.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
elig <- df[df$eligible_kpi_flag == 1, ]
groups <- list(elig$week_start, elig$weekend_flag)
on_time <- tapply(elig$on_time_kpi_flag, groups, sum)      # rows = weeks, columns = 0/1
n <- tapply(elig$on_time_kpi_flag, groups, length)
rate <- 100 * on_time / n
for (week in rownames(on_time)) {
  cat(week, sprintf("weekday %d/%d = %.1f%% | weekend %d/%d = %.1f%%\n",
                    on_time[week, "0"], n[week, "0"], rate[week, "0"],
                    on_time[week, "1"], n[week, "1"], rate[week, "1"]))
}
cat("Question: does this show that weekend staffing *caused* the dip?\n")
cat("What else differs on weekends?\n")

* Extension: latest-week on-time deliveries by region, with each denominator.
* Run the import block first so OrdersStory is open.
DATASET ACTIVATE OrdersStory.
TEMPORARY.
SELECT IF (week_start=DATE.DMY(24,8,2026) AND eligible_kpi_flag=1).
CROSSTABS
  /TABLES=region BY on_time_kpi_flag
  /CELLS=COUNT ROW.
Python Parts L

Break the latest week into the four regions with their denominators. Are the differences large compared with the size of each group?

# Extension: latest-week on-time rate by region, with each denominator.
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("orders_story.csv")
is_latest = df["week_start"] == df["week_start"].max()
latest = df[(df["eligible_kpi_flag"] == 1) & is_latest]
by_region = latest.groupby("region").agg(on_time=("on_time_kpi_flag", "sum"),
                                         n=("order_id", "size"))
by_region["rate"] = (by_region["on_time"] / by_region["n"]).map("{:.1%}".format)
print(by_region.to_string())
print(f"Check: the four n values add to {by_region['n'].sum()} (should be {len(latest)}).")
print("Question: is any region far from the others, or are the gaps small next to n?")
R Parts L

The same breakdown in base R with aggregate(). The four n values should add to 500.

# Extension: latest-week on-time rate by region, with each denominator.
df <- read.csv("orders_story.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
latest <- df[df$eligible_kpi_flag == 1 & df$week_start == max(df$week_start), ]
by_region <- aggregate(cbind(on_time = on_time_kpi_flag, n = eligible_kpi_flag) ~ region,
                       data = latest, FUN = sum)
by_region$rate <- sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * by_region$on_time / by_region$n)
print(by_region)
cat("Check: the four n values should add to", nrow(latest), "\n")
cat("Question: is any region far from the others, or are the gaps small next to n?\n")

Topic 4 · How late are the late deliveries, week by week? Extend

Same question in Excel → SPSS → Python → R.

Excel Parts L

In a copy of your workbook, add a new sheet. In A2 type =DATE(2026,8,3), in A3 type =A2+7 and fill down to A5. In B2 type =COUNTIFS(Orders[week_start],A2,Orders[late_minutes],">0"). In C2 type =AVERAGEIFS(Orders[late_minutes],Orders[week_start],A2,Orders[late_minutes],">0"). In D2 type =MEDIAN(FILTER(Orders[late_minutes],(Orders[week_start]=A2)*(Orders[late_minutes]>0))), and in E2 type =PERCENTILE.INC(FILTER(Orders[late_minutes],(Orders[week_start]=A2)*(Orders[late_minutes]>0)),0.9). Fill row 2 down to row 5. Every row in this file is eligible (Part K), so no eligibility test is needed here. The latest week should match KPI_Build row 18: 108, 12.4, 7 and 31.

SPSS Parts L

EXAMINE describes the late deliveries in each week, with medians, 90th percentiles and boxplots. SPSS uses a different percentile rule from PERCENTILE.INC, so small differences from Excel are expected.

New code: paste it at the end of S02P_SPSS.sps, make sure the setup has run this session, then select only the pasted lines and choose Run › Selection.

* Extension: late minutes week by week, for late deliveries only.
* Run the import block first so OrdersStory is open.
DATASET ACTIVATE OrdersStory.
TEMPORARY.
SELECT IF (eligible_kpi_flag=1 AND late_minutes>0).
EXAMINE VARIABLES=late_minutes BY week_start
  /PLOT=BOXPLOT
  /STATISTICS=DESCRIPTIVES
  /PERCENTILES(50,90)
  /NOTOTAL.
Python Parts L

Summarize late minutes week by week and save a boxplot as a PNG. The latest week should show n = 108, mean 12.4, median 7 and 90th percentile 31.

# Extension: mean, median and 90th percentile of late minutes for every week.
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")                     # save to file; no window needed
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("orders_story.csv")
late = df[(df["eligible_kpi_flag"] == 1) & (df["late_minutes"] > 0)]
summary = late.groupby("week_start")["late_minutes"].agg(
    n="size", mean="mean", median="median",
    p90=lambda x: x.quantile(0.9))        # same as PERCENTILE.INC
print(summary.round(1).to_string())

weeks = sorted(late["week_start"].unique())
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.boxplot([late.loc[late["week_start"] == w, "late_minutes"] for w in weeks])
ax.set_xticks(range(1, len(weeks) + 1), weeks)
ax.set_ylabel("Minutes late"); ax.set_title("Late deliveries by week")
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("late_minutes_boxplot.png", dpi=150)
print("Saved late_minutes_boxplot.png")
print("Question: in which week is the mean furthest above the median?")
print("What does that suggest?")
R Parts L

The same summary in base R, with a boxplot. In which week is the mean furthest above the median?

# Extension: mean, median and 90th percentile of late minutes for every week.
df <- read.csv("orders_story.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
late <- df[df$eligible_kpi_flag == 1 & df$late_minutes > 0, ]
summ <- function(x) {
  c(n = length(x), mean = round(mean(x), 1), median = median(x),
    p90 = quantile(x, 0.9, type = 7, names = FALSE))      # type 7 = PERCENTILE.INC
}
out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(late$late_minutes, late$week_start), summ))
print(out)
boxplot(late_minutes ~ week_start, data = late, ylab = "Minutes late",
        main = "Late deliveries by week")
cat("Question: in which week is the mean furthest above the median?\n")
cat("What does that suggest?\n")

Topic 5 · An average of rates versus the rate from counts Extend

Same question in Excel → SPSS → Python → R.

Excel Parts D

In a copy of your workbook, go to Slide_Practice and make the latest week twice as big: change B24 from 392 to 784 and B28 from 500 to 1000 (its rate is still 78.4%). In an empty cell type =AVERAGE(B21/B25,B22/B26,B23/B27,B24/B28). It still shows 83.75%, but B34 drops to 82.68%. Which one counts every delivery once?

SPSS Parts D

This block types its own numbers, like Hand-off Block H2, and opens a new small dataset. DESCRIPTIVES gives the mean of the four rates, 83.75%. AGGREGATE sums the counts first and gives 82.68%.

New code: paste it at the end of S02P_SPSS.sps, make sure the setup has run this session, then select only the pasted lines and choose Run › Selection.

* Extension: an average of rates can hide unequal week sizes.
* This block types its own numbers, like Hand-off Block H2.
* The latest week is made twice as big. Its rate is still 78.4%.
NEW FILE.
DATA LIST FREE / week (A10) ontime eligible.
BEGIN DATA
2026-08-03 420 500
2026-08-10 438 500
2026-08-17 425 500
2026-08-24 784 1000
END DATA.
COMPUTE rate=ontime/eligible.
FORMATS rate (PCT6.2).
LIST.

* Route 1: average the four rates. Each week counts once.
DESCRIPTIVES VARIABLES=rate
  /STATISTICS=MEAN.

* Route 2: sum the counts, then divide. Each delivery counts once.
AGGREGATE
 /OUTFILE=*
 /BREAK=
 /ontime_total=SUM(ontime)
 /eligible_total=SUM(eligible).
COMPUTE overall_rate=ontime_total/eligible_total.
FORMATS overall_rate (PCT6.2).
LIST.
Python Parts D

Types the same four weeks with the latest week doubled. You should see 83.75% for the average of rates and 2067 / 2500 = 82.68% from the counts.

# Extension: watch an average of rates go wrong when weeks have different sizes.
# The latest week is made twice as big (784 of 1000). Its rate is still 78.4%.
on_time = [420, 438, 425, 784]
eligible = [500, 500, 500, 1000]

rates = [o / e for o, e in zip(on_time, eligible)]
print("Weekly rates:", ", ".join(f"{r:.1%}" for r in rates))

average_of_rates = sum(rates) / len(rates)        # each week counts once
rate_from_counts = sum(on_time) / sum(eligible)   # each delivery counts once
print(f"Average of the four rates : {average_of_rates:.2%}")
print(f"Sum counts, then divide   : {sum(on_time)} / {sum(eligible)} "
      f"= {rate_from_counts:.2%}")
print("Question: which number counts every delivery once?")
R Parts D

The same two routes in base R. You should see 83.75% and 82.68%.

# Extension: watch an average of rates go wrong when weeks have different sizes.
# Base R only. The latest week is made twice as big (784 of 1000).
# Its rate is still 78.4%.
on_time <- c(420, 438, 425, 784)
eligible <- c(500, 500, 500, 1000)

rates <- on_time / eligible
cat("Weekly rates:", sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * rates), "\n")
# Route 1: each week counts once.
cat(sprintf("Average of the four rates : %.2f%%\n", 100 * mean(rates)))
# Route 2: each delivery counts once.
cat(sprintf("Sum counts, then divide   : %d / %d = %.2f%%\n",
            sum(on_time), sum(eligible), 100 * sum(on_time) / sum(eligible)))
cat("Question: which number counts every delivery once?\n")
